question: One replica apart: B=64 takes XLA's 4-wide path (v2(5)+v2(64)=6) and B=65 stays scalar (v2(5)+v2(65)=0). Does the rule hold across independent sessions and devices?
design: Identical code on every platform -- sim_core.py and pair_test.py embedded in the Kaggle notebook with their SHA-256 verified byte-for-byte against the repository. Arms INTERLEAVED (64,65,64,65,...) so drift cannot load onto one arm. Compilation outside the timer. 40 temperatures x 1500 sweeps = 60,000 sweeps per cell.

kaggle_t4.verdict: Four independent Kaggle sessions on four physical T4s, three interleaved repeats each. Every account separates with no overlap, the penalties span only 3.1 pp, and globally the slowest B=65 is far below the fastest B=64.

h100_pair.note: Three independent containers, three physical H100s, three interleaved repeats each. They agree with each other, so this is not noise.

h100_control.harness: app.py::stride_discriminator --lattices ref, the path that produced +12.1%
h100_control.harness_validated: B=63 gives 2.216 against 2.2121 measured earlier (+0.18%) and B=64 gives 2.538 against 2.5354 (+0.10%), so the harness reproduces the old numbers.
h100_control.diagnosis: B=65 is genuinely slow on this device: 2.438 against 2.216 for B=63, a +10% gap between two batches of the SAME width. The rule does not explain that -- it is the broad sawtooth, which has no mechanism.
h100_control.lesson: An isolated pair is a WEAK experiment. It works when the effect dominates the background wobble (the T4 at +80%) and fails when it does not. On an H100 the same B=64 measures +14.5% or +4.1% depending on which odd batch it is compared against, and the difference is the sawtooth, not the effect. The serious measurements are dense contiguous windows of 8 to 17 batches.
